title: Why Every Chatbot Gives You the Same 'Random' Number
hook: Ask any major chatbot for a random number between 1 and 10, and you'll almost always get 7. It's a small window into a bigger problem: AI models trained the same way tend to think alike.
key_points: Ask Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini for 'a random number between 1 and 10' and the answer is overwhelmingly 7.
A study asking 25 different LLMs to write a metaphor about time got mostly variations of 'time is a river' or 'time is a weaver.'
The cause: most LLMs are trained in similar ways on similar data, so they converge on the same likely answers.
Simply cranking up 'randomness' (temperature) doesn't fix it — it just makes replies incoherent.
One startup's fix: add unpredictability only at specific words, not the whole reply, to stay varied and coherent.
content_html: Try this: ask your chatbot of choice for a random number between 1 and 10. You'll almost certainly get 7. Ask again and you'll likely get 3 or 4, then 8 or 9 — a narrow, predictable range dressed up as randomness. MIT Technology Review calls this "groupthink," and the number game is just the most shareable example of something researchers have measured more rigorously: when 25 different LLMs were each asked 50 times to write a metaphor about time, most of the answers boiled down to "time is a river" or "time is a weaver."
extra_html: The cause isn't a bug in any one model — it's that most large language models are trained in similar ways, on similar data, to do similar tasks, so they tend to converge on the same statistically likely answers. The obvious fix, turning up the model's "temperature" (its randomness setting), doesn't really work: crank it up globally and replies start to fall apart into nonsense, trading groupthink for incoherence. One attempted solution, from the Australian startup Springboards, targets the problem more precisely: its tool, built on an open-source model, only injects extra unpredictability at specific points in a response — like the moment just before naming a travel destination — rather than throughout. The result, the company claims, is answers that are both more varied and still make sense. For everyday users, the underlying lesson is a useful corrective to how capable these tools feel: convincing, fluent answers aren't the same as original ones, and a model's "creativity" is often narrower than it appears.

related.title: How a Language Model Works
related.hook: A chatbot isn't reading and thinking — it's running the world's most sophisticated autocomplete, picking each next word from probabilities learned across billions of sentences.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

flashcards.prompt: If you ask a chatbot for 'a random number between 1 and 10,' what will you most likely get?

choices.text: 7 — nearly every major chatbot defaults to it
A genuinely random number each time

flashcards.explanation_html: Despite being asked for randomness, major LLMs overwhelmingly answer "7," revealing how predictable their "random" outputs really are.

flashcards.prompt: Why do different chatbots (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) converge on similar answers?
flashcards.back_html: They're trained in similar ways on similar data to do similar tasks, so they tend to land on the same high-probability answers.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't you just fix this by cranking up the model's 'randomness' (temperature)?

choices.text: Turning up randomness broadly makes replies incoherent, not just more varied
Chatbots don't have a randomness setting
It would make the model too slow to use

flashcards.explanation_html: Temperature is a blunt tool — pushed too high across the board, it trades predictable answers for garbled, incoherent ones rather than useful variety.

flashcards.back_html: Instead of adding randomness everywhere, it targets specific points in a reply — like just before naming a destination — so the rest stays coherent.
